title: Advanced trait boundaries without accidental complexity
summary: Use associated types, dyn compatibility, higher-ranked bounds and const generics only where the contract needs them.
objectives: Explain coherence, orphan rules and dyn compatibility
Use higher-ranked lifetime bounds with a borrowing callback
Distinguish type-level sizes from runtime lengths
body:
Purpose: express the needed relationship

An abstraction earns its place by making an important relationship explicit. A source produces one kind of item; a callback can borrow different inputs; a fixed-size packet has a length known to its type. These are useful constraints. They are not reasons to turn every function into a generic framework. This specialization is for library and systems boundaries that genuinely need these relationships.

Plain model: a contract has several dimensions

A trait's associated type lets an implementation choose an output type once. Our Source trait associates an Item with each source. A Countdown implements it with u8. A trait generic parameter instead permits different implementations for different parameter choices where coherence allows them. Choose the representation that reflects who makes the choice.

A dyn Source<Item = u8> is a trait object: the caller knows the interface and item type, while the concrete implementation is selected at runtime. Dynamic dispatch uses an indirect method call through implementation metadata. A generic function can use static dispatch and compiler specialization for concrete types. The performance difference depends on inlining, code size, memory access and workload; do not claim one always wins.

Prediction: can any trait become dyn?

A trait has fn encode<T>(&self, value: T). Can a single runtime method entry stand for every possible T? Predict the diagnostic when compiling exercises/specializations/dyn.rs.

Prediction explained

This method has an unconstrained family of type-specialized implementations, so the trait is not dyn-compatible as written. The Reference calls this dyn compatibility, formerly object safety. A method restricted with where Self: Sized can be excluded from the object interface, or a concrete input type can make the needed operation dispatchable. The right fix depends on what callers need.

Run and inspect the specialization lab

Working directory projects/:

mise exec -- cargo run -p rust-specializations --example dispatch
mise exec -- cargo test -p rust-specializations

The example prints a derived type name, a countdown sequence and a borrowed first word. The sequence is [2, 1, 0] for an initial count of 3; it stops before unsigned underflow. The reference uses checked subtraction because reaching zero is normal completion, not a programmer failure.

Follow the type relationships

with_first accepts a callback bounded by for<'b> Fn(&'b str) -> &'b str. The for quantifies the lifetime: the callback must work for every input borrow lifetime rather than requiring one specific captured lifetime. It returns a slice tied to the input it receives. This is useful when a library repeatedly lends different temporary inputs to user code. It does not extend any input's lifetime.

Packet<T, const N: usize> stores an array whose size is part of the type. Packet<u8, 4> and Packet<u8, 8> are different types. This can express wire-size or hardware constraints, but it can also generate many instantiations and complicate APIs. A slice is often the appropriate choice for runtime-variable inputs. N = 0 is a valid case unless the contract explicitly excludes it; test it.

Pattern ergonomics infer borrowing in patterns matched against references. For example, matching a borrowed Option can bind a borrowed inner value without moving it. Edition 2024 tightens which explicit binding modifiers are allowed when the default binding mode has already become a reference. When confused, write the scrutinee's type and the binding's type. A pattern changes how you access the value; it does not create ownership from nowhere.

Intentional failure: implementing someone else's trait for someone else's type

Compile exercises/specializations/orphan.rs with rustc from the course root. It attempts to implement standard Display for standard Vec. The expected E0117 illustrates the orphan rules. Those rules help make trait resolution coherent across independently authored crates. A local newtype wrapper gives your crate a type whose formatting contract it owns.

mise exec -- rustc --edition 2024 exercises/specializations/orphan.rs

This file is intentionally rejected and listed in the expected-error manifest. It is never part of a successful project build. The supported correction is a local wrapper plus a Display implementation, not weakening compiler checks.

Guided checkpoint

Read the Source trait and Countdown implementation, then call drain through the trait object. Next change the caller to a generic function over S: Source<Item = u8> in your learner branch. Keep behavior tests identical. Explain which choice moves type selection to compile time and which supports a heterogeneous collection of implementations. Do not add a benchmark unless performance is an actual decision criterion.

Independent practice and hints

Implement a bounded slice source yielding borrowed items. Choose whether its Item is a reference and explain the lifetime. Wrap a Vec of bytes in a local type that prints its length without exposing contents. Add a zero-capacity Packet test.

Hint 1

The source struct can hold a slice and current index. Ownership of the backing allocation stays with the caller.

Hint 2

Use get and return Option at exhaustion. A reference item can carry the lifetime parameter from the source struct.

Reference direction

A source borrowing &'a [T] can yield &'a T by incrementing an index after a successful get. A local Bytes wrapper implements Display with a length-only message. These avoid cloning the payload and avoid a trait implementation that violates coherence. If the API must mutate or lend each item for a shorter borrow, a generic associated type may be the next requirement; do not introduce it before that need exists.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The lab isolates three real type relationships in one small crate and uses the standard library for its runtime behavior. Its tests check exhaustion, borrowed output, generic derive parameters and zero-sized arrays. Static and dynamic dispatch are alternatives with different extensibility and code-generation tradeoffs, not a hierarchy of professionalism. The verification log records actual checks; it contains no unmeasured dispatch speed claim. A new requirement for heterogeneous plugins would justify retaining dynamic dispatch; a tiny hot loop might justify a measured generic variant.

Playbook investigation: “the lifetime annotation owns the text”

Observed: returning a slice from a locally created String fails even after adding a named lifetime. Hypothesis A: the annotation forces the String to live longer. Hypothesis B: it only describes a borrowing relationship. Replace the local String with an input reference carrying that lifetime. If the input-based version compiles and the local version does not, A is disproved. The sound alternatives are returning owned data or borrowing from an owner that actually outlives the return value.

When you get stuck

Write the missing contract

Reduce to one trait method and one call. Annotate the concrete type, associated type and reference lifetime separately. Run mise exec -- rustc --explain E0038 for dyn compatibility or E0117 for coherence, then compare with the pinned compiler's Reference.

Mastery check

Explain why one proposed abstraction is unnecessary for a calculator but useful for a plugin boundary. Modify the lab and diagnose both expected failures without copying the reference. Show a hypothesis you revised and distinguish compilation evidence from API usability evidence.

title: Macros generate code, not correctness
summary: Build and inspect one declarative macro and one narrowly scoped derive.
objectives: Reason about evaluation count, hygiene and generated bounds
Review compile-time dependencies and API evolution
body:
Purpose: remove repetition without hiding the contract

Macros are useful when the repeated structure is syntax rather than an ordinary runtime value. A derive can produce an implementation for a declared type. A declarative macro can accept a repeated list of expressions. Neither mechanism makes the generated code correct by definition. It creates another source of code that must be read and tested.

Plain model: transformation before ordinary checking

A declarative macro matches tokens against patterns and expands to Rust syntax. A procedural macro is compiled host code that consumes and returns token streams. The compiler then checks the expanded program. Procedural macros are build-time dependencies capable of executing code during compilation, so dependency review matters even when the final program has a small runtime surface.

Use a function when a function expresses the need. A function has ordinary parameter types, return types and call behavior. Use a macro only when its syntax or generated implementation provides a concrete benefit. Our checked_sum example accepts any number of expressions and emits a checked accumulation. The TypeName-like derive implements one small, stable trait without duplicating generic parameter handling at every type.

Predict evaluation count

A macro invocation supplies two expressions that each increment a counter. What must be true for the counter to end at two rather than four? If the first addition overflows, should the second supplied expression still be evaluated? Predict the current reference's explicit policy before reading it.

Prediction explained

The macro stores each supplied expression in a local before using it, so each is evaluated once, left to right. It still evaluates later expressions after an earlier overflow because expansion contains those let statements. The arithmetic result remains None. That evaluation policy is part of the API; a short-circuit alternative could be valid but must be documented and tested.

Run the macro lab

Working directory projects/: mise exec -- cargo test -p rust-specializations macro_once_and_overflow. Inspect checked_sum! in the actual source. The test checks both the returned sum and the side-effect count, so it guards a property that a result-only test would miss.

Source with both macro consumer and trait examples

Read the declarative expansion

$value:expr matches one expression. The repetition accepts comma-separated expressions and an optional trailing comma. Double braces make the result a block expression with its own local names. Each next value is constrained to i64. and_then combines a prior successful total with checked addition. It preserves None after overflow without wrapping or panicking.

Macro hygiene helps prevent accidental interaction between generated local bindings and caller names, but it is not a universal promise about every path. Exported macros should use deliberate paths, often $crate for their own crate's items. Our example uses no helper items beyond language and standard prelude names. If you generalize it, test expansion in a separate consumer crate rather than only inside the defining module.

The procedural derive

The crate has proc-macro = true and runs on the compiler host, even when the consuming crate targets WASM. The maintained syn parser converts tokens into a DeriveInput. This avoids inventing a partial Rust parser. quote constructs output tokens while preserving Rust identifiers. split_for_impl separates declaration parameters, use-site arguments and where clauses; omitting those would break generic consumers.

The generated implementation names crate::KindName. This is an intentional lab contract: the consuming crate defines that trait at its root. A reusable published derive should usually target a documented companion trait crate and account for renamed dependencies. The explicit restriction is more honest than claiming a tiny derive is universally portable.

Deliberate mistake: repeating an expression

In a learner copy, use the supplied expression twice in an expansion, such as once to log and once to add. Run the side-effect test. A macro can type-check while changing how many times the caller's operation runs. The sound correction binds the expression once and reuses the value or reference according to its ownership needs. Do not merely remove the failing test.

Guided checkpoint

First run the handwritten KindName implementation on a simple struct. Then replace that exact implementation with the derive and preserve the same observable test. Next test Packet<T, N> so generic arguments and const parameters pass through. Finally add a where-constrained type. Each step expands the supported syntax with a concrete test; it does not claim to support arbitrary advanced syntax by inspection alone.

Independent work and tiered hints

Add a documented empty invocation behavior to checked_sum, then test a caller variable named total. Design a compile-fail consumer where the required trait is absent and explain whether the resulting diagnostic is clear enough. Propose one improvement without hiding errors behind a catch-all panic.

Hint 1

The identity value for a sum is zero, but the output type should remain explicit. The macro's local variable should not mutate the caller's similarly named variable.

Hint 2

Generated code errors point into expansion or invocation spans. A procedural macro can report a structured syn error for unsupported input rather than panicking.

Reference direction

Specify Some(0i64) for no values and assert the caller's total is unchanged after a nonempty call. If the derive's trait path is part of the supported contract, document it next to installation instructions. A fuller library can accept a helper attribute naming the trait path and parse it with syn; that is a new requirement, not a reason to complicate this lab preemptively.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The procedural macro depends on exact syn 3.0.9 and quote 1.0.47 because parsing Rust syntax and preserving token structure are concrete requirements. The ordinary runtime examples remain standard-library based. Tests cover single evaluation, overflow, generic and const parameter preservation. A downstream compile-fail test would add evidence about diagnostics; the manifest must not imply one ran unless its command is recorded. An ordinary function is the preferred alternative when token-level flexibility is unnecessary.

Playbook investigation: the derive breaks only generic types

Observed: a unit struct derives successfully, but Packet<u8,4> fails with missing generics. Hypothesis A: derives cannot support const generics. Hypothesis B: the expansion discarded type arguments. Write the equivalent handwritten impl. If it compiles, A is disproved. Inspect generated syntax or the quote expression and restore the split generic pieces. Re-run both simple and generic cases; fixing one must not silently narrow the other.

When you get stuck

Reduce the generated program

Write the expansion you expect as ordinary Rust in a temporary test crate. Compile it before debugging token construction. Provide the input, expected expansion and earliest compiler error to a reviewer. Prefer current official macro documentation over random examples using an incompatible syn major version.

Mastery check

Explain evaluation order, ownership and the trait-path limitation without reading the macro body. Diagnose a double-evaluation defect and justify whether a new request belongs in a function, a declarative macro or a derive. Passing the expansion test is one piece of that judgment.

title: Foreign interfaces and environments without std
summary: Make contracts explicit when Rust meets C or a target without an operating system.
objectives: Explain ABI, ownership and unwinding at FFI boundaries
Audit a tiny safe FFI wrapper
Distinguish no_std, allocation and embedded target support
body:
Purpose: know what Rust cannot check for you

Rust code sometimes calls a library written in another language or runs on a target without an operating system. The compiler still checks Rust types and borrowing, but it cannot infer a foreign function's full contract or invent a hardware runtime. This specialization teaches how to make that missing contract explicit. It is not a prerequisite for every web application.

Plain model: agreeing on the boundary

An application binary interface, or ABI, specifies machine-level calling conventions such as parameter passing and symbol naming. An extern declaration tells Rust how a foreign function is expected to behave at that boundary. It is a claim made by the programmer. A wrong declaration can compile and still cause undefined behavior when called.

For pointer-based APIs, the contract must include validity, alignment, length, initialization, aliasing, ownership and duration. Does the function retain a pointer after returning? Who frees it, with which allocator? May it call back on another thread? Can it unwind? A null check does not answer those questions. Start with an established binding crate and vendor documentation when possible rather than writing broad declarations by guesswork.

Prediction: an innocent absolute value

The C function abs accepts a signed int. What happens for the most negative int, whose positive magnitude does not fit in the same signed type? Would wrapping its call inside a safe Rust function automatically make every input safe?

Prediction explained

A safe wrapper must prevent inputs that violate the foreign contract. C signed abs of the unrepresentable minimum has undefined behavior. The wrapper explicitly returns None before making that call. Calling a foreign function from safe-looking syntax does not repair an invalid precondition.

Run the narrow wrapper test

Working directory projects/: mise exec -- cargo test -p rust-specializations ffi_boundary. The course verifies this host ABI example on the recorded macOS target. Porting it requires checking that the C library exposes the declared symbol and compatible int representation on the new target.

The source's unsafe extern "C" block declares abs. c_int expresses the platform C int type. The wrapper rejects its minimum, then documents the proof immediately above the unsafe call. The safe baseline is Rust's checked_abs(). Ordinary Rust code should use that baseline; the foreign call exists only to teach a boundary that actual C integrations need.

Deliberate mistake: a wrapper without its guard

Do not run an unchecked minimum-input call as an ordinary demonstration. Undefined behavior is not an expected panic or a useful stable output. Instead, review a learner diff that removes the guard and identify the violated precondition. The safe test suite compares all supported representative inputs to the standard-library baseline and verifies the excluded case returns None. Tests exercise selected inputs; the written contract covers the entire intended input set.

Guided checkpoint: write the contract before the extern

In a learner branch, write a comment containing symbol name, ABI, input validity, output relation and failure representation. Implement the safe baseline first. Add the foreign declaration, guard and unsafe call only after the contract is clear. Keep the unsafe block as small as possible. Test zero, positive, negative, maximum and minimum inputs. Explain why each is chosen.

For a hypothetical buffer API, stop before implementation and write who owns the allocation and whether the foreign code keeps the pointer. Returning a Rust slice requires the referent to remain valid for the promised lifetime; an extern signature cannot supply that proof. Do not let a panic cross a boundary whose ABI does not permit unwinding. A maintained library may already encapsulate this complexity more reliably than a new wrapper.

What no_std does and does not mean

#![no_std] asks a crate to depend on core instead of automatically using the full standard library. Core provides fundamental types and algorithms that do not require operating-system services. An optional alloc crate can provide allocation-backed structures when a suitable allocator exists. no_std does not mean no heap, no panic, no unsafe or automatically suitable for every microcontroller.

A library is not a complete embedded executable. The executable needs a target, startup code, memory layout, panic behavior, often an interrupt model, and hardware-specific support. Peripheral access may involve volatile operations and device rules that ordinary RAM reasoning does not capture. Those target-specific requirements are outside this portable host lab.

Run mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path exercises/specializations/no-std/Cargo.toml from the course root. This checks the pure transform using a host test harness. It does not flash hardware or verify timing, interrupts, power behavior or an embedded linker script.

Independent practice with hints

Extend the no_std transform with a checked calibration offset. Decide whether saturation or an error is correct for the stated sensor requirement. Then review a fictional C API that returns an owned buffer and requires a matching free function. Draw ownership from allocation to Drop before writing code.

Hint 1

“Never exceeds the display's range” and “must report an invalid measurement” are different contracts. Both saturation and errors can be appropriate under different requirements.

Hint 2

Model a foreign allocation with an owning wrapper whose Drop calls exactly the documented deallocator. Borrowed views cannot outlive that wrapper. A retained callback needs a separate lifetime and thread contract.

Reference approach

For an error-reporting sensor, checked addition returns Option or a domain Result and leaves invalid measurements distinguishable from maximum valid ones. For a display-only bounded gauge, saturation may be the correct visible policy. The C buffer wrapper needs length and pointer validity checks plus one owner; use a maintained crate if available. The ownership diagram is a design exercise, not a verified generic wrapper supplied by this course.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The executable FFI example has no pointer or allocator contract and excludes one invalid integer. That is a deliberately small proof obligation. The no_std example has no dependencies and no allocation because its operation needs neither. Actual host tests and compiler checks are recorded separately. Miri generally cannot execute arbitrary native foreign functions; its successful checks on the separate unsafe Rust buffer do not validate this C library. A real embedded target or pointer API justifies a new target-specific verification plan.

Playbook investigation: “no_std means this is a firmware image”

Observation: a library checks successfully but cannot be flashed as an application. Hypothesis A: the arithmetic transform is wrong. Hypothesis B: there is no executable entry point, linker layout or hardware target. Inspect Cargo's target kind and produced artifact before editing the function. If it is a library archive with no startup contract, A does not explain the missing image. The next sound step is to select documented board support and a minimal executable, not add random unsafe operations.

When you get stuck

Boundary report

Record target triple, compiler, C header/library version, ABI declaration, ownership diagram and the smallest linking command. For hardware, add board and linker information. Seek domain review when pointer, interrupt or allocator contracts are unclear; repeated host tests cannot substitute for missing expertise.

Mastery check

Explain every unsafe precondition in the wrapper and why the safe baseline is preferred in ordinary code. Distinguish what the no_std host test establishes from what a real device needs. Reject a proposed wrapper that hides missing lifetime evidence behind an invented static reference.

Current stable FFI capabilities

Rust 1.99 supports defining C and C-unwind variadic functions, in addition to calling foreign variadic functions. This does not validate the argument count, promoted argument types, ABI, or ownership contract for you. Prefer fixed signatures for new interfaces where possible. The course retains a fixed-signature host example so its safety argument stays small. Rust 1.99.1 also corrects an x86_64 FFI bool-return regression; compiler patch versions can affect ABI correctness without adding language syntax.
